title: Nearly quadratic oracle complexity for convex-body volume
formal: Is there a randomized classical membership-oracle algorithm such that, for every fixed \(a\ge1\), every \(n\ge2\), and every convex body \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) with \(B_2^n\subseteq K\subseteq n^a B_2^n\), it returns \(V\) satisfying \[\Pr[|V-\operatorname{vol}_n(K)|\le\operatorname{vol}_n(K)/10]\ge2/3\] using at most \(C_a n^2(\log(2+n))^{c_a}\) membership queries in expectation? The polynomial-radius promise and origin are supplied; no isotropic position or uniform-sampling oracle is given.
definitions:
A convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior, and \(B_2^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_2\le1\}\). Volume means n-dimensional Lebesgue measure. More generally, supplied concentric radii \(r,R\) and center \(z\), with \(R/r\le n^a\), can be rescaled to this normalization; volume scales by \(r^n\). The exponent \(a\) is fixed independently of dimension, and the constants may depend on it.

The only access to the unknown body is the exact bit indicating whether a queried real point belongs to \(K\), including its boundary. Queries can be adaptive and randomized. The information model permits measurable choices of exact real points and arbitrary measurable computation between queries, all of which are uncharged. Every membership answer costs one query. No separation, optimization, boundary, quantum-superposition or conditional-sampling oracle is available. Randomness belongs to the algorithm; the body itself is adversarially fixed.

The algorithm must terminate almost surely. Both its expected query bound and success guarantee hold for each eligible body. An expected bound is the selected interpretation of oracle complexity, rather than a bound on every random tape. Preprocessing, rounding and production of auxiliary samples must pay for all membership queries they use. In particular, one cannot assume an isotropic transformation has already been found for free.

The relative accuracy \(1/10\) and probability \(2/3\) are fixed constants in the computational task. The atlas's absolute \(1/100\) rule for numerical answers does not replace this algorithmic success condition. The target bounds information from the oracle, not total arithmetic operations or the bit length needed to represent continuously distributed query points.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of an algorithm with the stated uniform relative-accuracy and expected-query guarantees, or its negation in the classical query model. A bound assuming free isotropic rounding, a quantum algorithm, or an estimate for a constant-dimensional high-precision regime does not suffice. A matching-order lower bound alone does not prove the requested upper bound.
context:
The corrected Jia–Laddha–Lee–Vempala revision gives a general membership-oracle volume bound with a roughly n^(7/2) rounding term and an n^3 accuracy term, up to logarithms. This remains above the target at fixed accuracy.

Vempala’s September 2026 preprint states a nearly quadratic lower bound for constant-factor volume estimation even with polynomially bounded radius ratio. It supports the relevance of a quadratic target but does not supply an algorithm.

A separate October 2026 preprint improves quantum volume-query bounds. Its quantum membership access is stronger than the classical bit-answer interface fixed here.
why: This targets the dimension dependence of a fundamental randomized integration problem.

import_provenance.original_title: Nearly quadratic oracle complexity for convex-body volume
import_provenance.original_statement: Can a randomized algorithm estimate the volume of an n-dimensional convex body to fixed relative error using O(n² polylog n) membership queries with success probability at least 2/3? Assume known concentric inner and outer balls with polynomial radius ratio; the goal is the optimal dimension dependence, not the fixed-dimension small-error regime.

The goal is a constant-relative-error estimate of its volume with constant success probability.
